html:
A stepped pyramid at the Maya city of Palenque, begun about 675 as the tomb of King Pakal the Great and finished by his son. It takes its name from the three large carved panels in the temple on top, one of the longest Maya texts known, written in Maya script. They list Palenque's kings and dates in the Long Count.

In 1948 the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed a stone slab in the temple floor with holes for lifting. Under it was a stairway packed with rubble. It took four seasons to clear. In 1952 he reached a chamber at the base of the pyramid holding Pakal's stone coffin, with its famous carved lid and a jade mask.

A narrow stone tube runs from the tomb up the stairs to the temple, perhaps as a channel for the dead king's spirit. The find changed ideas about Maya pyramids, which until then were thought to be temples only, unlike the tombs of Egypt.
